title: Destructors and RAII

notes: The constructor switches the motor on (acquire); the destructor switches it off (release).
The early return still switches the pump off: the destructor runs on every way out of the scope.
A pair of braces makes a scope; the fan stops at the closing brace.
Copying is deleted so two Motor objects can never think they control the same motor.

exercises.title: A sensor reading buffer
exercises.prompt:
Finish class ReadingBuffer, which owns a heap array of doubles.
ReadingBuffer(int capacity) allocates the array with new double[capacity] (capacity may be 0).
~ReadingBuffer() releases it with delete[].
bool add(double v) stores v and returns true, or returns false if the buffer is full.
int size() const is how many values were added; double average() const is their average, or 0 when empty.

tests.call: []{ ReadingBuffer b(3); b.add(2); b.add(4); return b.size(); }()
[]{ ReadingBuffer b(3); b.add(2); b.add(5); return b.average(); }()
[]{ ReadingBuffer b(2); b.add(1); b.add(2); return b.add(3); }()
tests.hint_if_fail: When count == capacity the buffer is full.

tests.call: []{ ReadingBuffer b(2); b.add(1); b.add(2); b.add(30); return b.average(); }()
[]{ ReadingBuffer b(0); bool ok = b.add(5); return std::to_string(ok) + "," + std::to_string(b.average()); }()
tests.hint_if_fail: A buffer of capacity 0 can't take anything, and an empty average is 0.

tests.why: Write a destructor that releases the array.
The array was made with new[], so free it with delete[].

hints: add: if (count == capacity) return false; data[count++] = v; return true;

exercises.title: A lock guard for a door
exercises.prompt: Door is given. Write class LockGuard: LockGuard(Door& d) locks the door (locked = true) and adds 1 to timesLocked; its destructor unlocks it (locked = false). Copying a LockGuard must not be allowed (= delete). The door must be unlocked again however the scope is left, even by an exception.

tests.call: []{ Door d; LockGuard g(d); return d.locked; }()
[]{ Door d; { LockGuard g(d); } return d.locked; }()
[]{ Door d; { LockGuard a(d); } { LockGuard b(d); } return d.timesLocked; }()
[]{ Door d; try { LockGuard g(d); throw 1; } catch (int) {} return std::to_string(d.locked) + std::to_string(d.timesLocked); }()

tests.why: Delete the copy constructor: LockGuard(const LockGuard&) = delete;

hints: Keep a reference to the door as a member: Door& door; set it in the initialiser list.
LockGuard(Door& d) : door(d) { door.locked = true; door.timesLocked++; }
~LockGuard() { door.locked = false; } and LockGuard(const LockGuard&) = delete;

exercises.title: A wave that cleans up

tests.call: []{ Wave w; w.spawn(10); w.spawn(25); return w.totalHealth(); }()
[]{ int before = Enemy::alive; { Wave w; w.spawn(10); w.spawn(20); } return Enemy::alive - before; }()
tests.hint_if_fail: When the Wave is destroyed its enemies must be deleted: write ~Wave().

tests.call: []{ int before = Enemy::alive; Wave w; w.spawn(10); w.spawn(20); w.clear(); return (Enemy::alive - before) * 10 + w.count(); }()
tests.hint_if_fail: clear() must delete each enemy before emptying the vector.

tests.call: []{ int before = Enemy::alive; { Wave w; w.spawn(1); w.clear(); w.spawn(2); w.spawn(3); if (w.totalHealth() != 5) return -1; } return Enemy::alive - before; }()

hints: clear(): for (Enemy* e : enemies) delete e; then enemies.clear();
The destructor can simply call clear().
totalHealth: add up e->hp for each Enemy* e.

quiz.q: When does a stack object's destructor run?
choices: At the end of its scope, however the scope is left
quiz.why: Leaving the scope (end, return, break, exception) destroys the object.

quiz.q: What does RAII mean in practice?
choices: The constructor acquires a resource and the destructor releases it
quiz.why: The object's lifetime controls the resource.

quiz.q: A class has only a std::vector and a std::string as members. Does it need a destructor?
choices: No: the members clean themselves up

quiz.q: A class owns a raw pointer and gets copied with the default copy. What goes wrong?
choices: Both copies delete the same memory: a double delete
quiz.why: The default copy copies the pointer, not what it points at.

quiz.q: Why put 'motor off' in a destructor rather than at the end of the function?
choices: It also runs on early returns and exceptions
quiz.why: Cleanup in the destructor can't be skipped by an unexpected way out.

cards.a: ~ClassName() { ... } with no parameters and no return type.
Constructor acquires, destructor releases, scope decides when.
T(const T&) = delete; T& operator=(const T&) = delete;

explain: Explain RAII in your own words, using something from a tool or robot (a motor, a file, a lock) as the resource.
